To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
MS is associated with an increased number of TNF‐alpha‐producing blood cells, and that this increase can be corrected by treatment with IFN-β.
MS is associated with an elevated number of blood TNF‐α and reduced numbers of IL‐6‐ and IL‐8‐secreting MNC, with a normalization of the TNF‐α/IL‐10 ratio by IFN‐β treatment.

IFN‐β therapy in patients with relapsing‐remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) normalizes the elevated TNF‐α and the decreased IL‐10 levels of blood mononuclear cells, and that IFN‐γ levels in blood mononuclear cell cultures are elevated in RRMS patients compared to controls, whereas IL‐6 levels were not significantly different.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the involvement of TNF and IL‐10 as well as IL‐6 and, to a lesser extent, IFN‐gamma in MS, and the possible role of IFN‐beta in correcting the imbalance between TNF and IL-10.
the hypothesis that the beneficial effects of treatment with IFNs in MS are mediated by the normalization of the imbalance between TNF‐α and IL‐10.
the role of cytokines in MS pathogenesis.
